group.title: Borrowed words
sources: Words and CEFR levels chosen by the authors from general knowledge of English; meanings, examples and sentences are original

Word-list licences checked 2026-10-25: CEFR-J Wordlist 1.5 (Tono Laboratory, TUFS; free with citation, A1-B2) and NGSL/NAWL (CC BY-SA 4.0) were not copied; Oxford 3000 and English Vocabulary Profile terms were not confirmed, so they were not used

words.meaning: A favor given in exchange for something else.
examples: The support was a {quid pro quo} for a future contract.
wrong: It was a quid pro quo, so nothing was expected in return.

words.meaning: Repeated so often that it becomes boring or annoying.
examples: He talked about his new car {ad nauseam}.
wrong: She mentioned it ad nauseam, just once in passing.

words.meaning: Complete freedom to act as you think best.
examples: The new director was given {carte blanche} to redesign the theater.
wrong: With carte blanche, she needed approval for every small decision.

words.meaning: Something already done that cannot be changed.
examples: By the time we heard about the merger, it was a {fait accompli}.
wrong: The fait accompli was still open for discussion and change.

words.meaning: A final blow that ends something.
examples: The late goal delivered the {coup de grace}.
wrong: The coup de grace was the first of many attacks.

words.meaning: A young, successful person whose bold behavior shocks others.
examples: He was the {enfant terrible} of the fashion world.
wrong: As the enfant terrible of the art scene, she never upset anyone.

words.meaning: A cheerful enjoyment of life.
examples: Her {joie de vivre} made every party fun.
wrong: His joie de vivre made him gloomy and tired of everything.

words.meaning: The ability to act smoothly and correctly in social situations.
examples: She handled the awkward guests with great {savoir-faire}.
wrong: His savoir-faire showed when he insulted every guest.

words.meaning: A pleasing quality that is hard to describe.
examples: The café has a certain {je ne sais quoi} that keeps people coming back.
wrong: Its je ne sais quoi was obvious and easy to put into words.

words.meaning: Letting things happen without interfering or controlling.
examples: The manager has a {laissez-faire} approach to office hours.
wrong: Her laissez-faire style meant she checked every detail herself.

words.meaning: A public admission that you were wrong.
examples: The CEO issued a {mea culpa} after the data leak.
wrong: In his mea culpa, he blamed everyone but himself.

words.meaning: A person who is no longer welcome somewhere.
examples: After the scandal, he became {persona non grata} at the club.
wrong: As persona non grata, she was the guest of honor everywhere.

words.meaning: Something that is absolutely necessary.
examples: Trust is the {sine qua non} of any partnership.
wrong: Funding was the sine qua non, so we started without any.

words.meaning: A person’s usual way of doing something.
examples: Arriving early and leaving quietly was his {modus operandi}.
wrong: Her modus operandi was something she had never done before.

words.meaning: Another side of a person’s character, or a second identity.
examples: On stage, the shy singer becomes her bold {alter ego}.
wrong: His alter ego was exactly the same as his everyday self.

words.meaning: Again and again without end.
examples: The list of complaints could go on {ad infinitum}.
wrong: The debate went on ad infinitum for exactly five minutes.

words.meaning: Done for free, especially professional work for the public good.
examples: The lawyer took the case on a {pro bono} basis.
wrong: Her pro bono work earned her a huge fee.

words.meaning: An area of knowledge or land that is unknown or unexplored.
examples: For most of us, quantum physics is {terra incognita}.
wrong: The town was terra incognita to him, since he had lived there for years.

words.meaning: Using exactly the same words.
examples: She repeated the speech {verbatim}.
wrong: He quoted her verbatim, changing most of her words.

words.meaning: Required by fashion or social custom.
examples: Black tie is {de rigueur} at the gala.
wrong: Formal dress was de rigueur, so everyone came in shorts.

words.meaning: People who have recently become rich and show it off.
examples: The resort attracted the {nouveau riche} with its gold taps.
wrong: The nouveau riche had been wealthy for ten generations.

words.meaning: A false name that a writer uses instead of their real one.
examples: She published her crime novels under a {nom de plume}.
wrong: His nom de plume was the real name printed on his birth certificate.

words.meaning: Because of that very fact.
examples: A forged signature is {ipso facto} grounds for rejection.
wrong: Being a member was ipso facto a reason, though it had no effect at all.

words.meaning: Enjoy the present and use your chances now.
examples: ’{Carpe diem},’ she said, and booked the trip that night.
wrong: He believed in carpe diem, so he put everything off for years.

words.meaning: In full control of your mind and able to think clearly.
examples: The judge decided the witness was fully {compos mentis}.
wrong: He was compos mentis, so he couldn’t understand a word.

words.meaning: While not present.
examples: The degree was awarded {in absentia} because she was abroad.
wrong: He was tried in absentia while standing in front of the judge.

words.meaning: The idea that privileged people should help others.
examples: Out of {noblesse oblige}, the family funded the village school.
wrong: Noblesse oblige meant the rich owed nothing to anyone.

words.meaning: A return to friendly relations between former rivals.
examples: The summit led to a {rapprochement} between the two countries.
wrong: The rapprochement made the two sides bitter enemies.

words.meaning: A strong feeling of loyalty and pride shared by a group.
examples: The long training built real {esprit de corps} in the crew.
wrong: Their esprit de corps showed when each member worked against the others.

words.meaning: A word or phrase with two meanings, one often rude or funny.
examples: The comedian’s script was full of {double entendres}.
wrong: The double entendre had only one obvious meaning.

words.meaning: A person who enjoys good food, drink and company.
examples: A true {bon vivant}, he knew every good restaurant in Paris.
wrong: As a bon vivant, he hated good food and parties.

words.meaning: A sincere, passionate appeal or protest.
examples: Her letter was a {cri de coeur} for better care for the elderly.
wrong: His cri de coeur was a cool, indifferent remark.

words.meaning: A small second home in a city, used only now and then.
examples: They keep a {pied-a-terre} in the city for theater nights.
wrong: Their pied-a-terre is the huge country house where they live all year.

words.meaning: All together, as one large group.
examples: The staff resigned {en masse} after the decision.
wrong: They left en masse, one person at a time over many years.

words.meaning: Being the best example of its kind.
examples: She is the storyteller {par excellence}.
wrong: He was the chef par excellence, though his cooking was the worst in town.

words.meaning: A person or thing you especially dislike.
examples: Bad grammar is the editor’s {bete noire}.
wrong: Jazz is his bete noire, so he listens to it all day with joy.

words.meaning: An outstanding performance or achievement.
examples: Her final solo was a {tour de force}.
wrong: The tour de force was a dull and clumsy effort.

words.meaning: The most important reason for someone or something to exist.
examples: Teaching was her {raison d’etre}.
wrong: Music is his raison d’etre, so he never thinks about it.

words.meaning: The greatest work of an artist or writer.
examples: Many consider the trilogy his {magnum opus}.
wrong: Her magnum opus was a minor sketch she quickly forgot.

words.meaning: Holding a role because of another position you have.
examples: The mayor is an {ex officio} member of the board.
wrong: She was an ex officio member, chosen by a public vote for her own sake.
